content:
Hi all, I've been learning Lean and playing around with tracking how many succ calls it takes to build a number from zero. I noticed something that's probably expected but I can't figure out the right way to think about it.
I gave Nat a cost counter — every succ costs one token. Works fine for small stuff. But then I tried building pow2 n through pure succ calls and compared it to the recursive definition:

structure PricedNat where
  val : Nat; cost : Nat

def succP (x : PricedNat) :=
  { val := x.val + 1, cost := x.cost + 1 }

def pow2 : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 1 | n + 1 => pow2 n + pow2 n

pow2 n and building the same number through pure succP calls are obviously equal as Nat, but the cost differs by an exponential factor.
I understand why this happens — the recursive definition compresses the construction. But I'm not sure where this cost difference is supposed to live conceptually. Is it just "you defined two different algorithms, of course they have different costs" and that's the end of it? Or is there a way to think about this that fits inside Lean's existing structure somehow?
Full code: https://gist.github.com/lihaoweiseven/603a37b8cf9b616d483e21fe7e16d78f
Not asking for changes, just trying to learn. Thanks!

FYI there is a channel #**new members>

I looked through your code and the main point is that
pow2 has nothing to do with your pricedNat, it is merely a function on the naturals. (i.e. just 2^n).
Therefore your last statement just says (after unfolding definitions), that n < 2 ^ n.

I assume you want to track the costs of the algorithm you used in pow2. For you to do this properly, you could (re)define addition on PricedNat.

def addPricedNat : PricedNat → PricedNat → PricedNat :=
    fun ⟨a, b⟩ ⟨c, d⟩ ↦
    match c with
    | 0 => ⟨a, b + d⟩
    | c + 1 => addPricedNat (succP ⟨a, b⟩) ⟨c, d⟩

instance : Add PricedNat where
  add := addPricedNat

**
Then you could define pow2 as a function from Nat to pricedNat (i.e. giving you both the 2^n value as well as the computational cost), i.e.

def pow2 : Nat → PricedNat
  | 0 => ⟨1, 1⟩
  | n + 1 => pow2 n + pow2 n

Thanks, that helps a lot. I think I see the bug in my example now: my pow2 was still just a Nat function, so PricedNat could not observe any cost unless I define the operations inside PricedNat too.

My remaining confusion is maybe more conceptual than about this toy encoding. If two definitions give the same Nat value, but one builds it through many more succ/add steps, is the usual Lean way to talk about that just to move to an instrumented type/monad like this? Or is there some standard terminology/library for the cost of the construction, separate from the Nat value itself?

Sorry if this is a basic question — I may be mixing up computation, definitions, and proofs here.

There's no general framework or foundational support for reasoning about the computational complexity of a Lean declaration (like a def) and definitely not relative to the output of the compiler as it will run on your machine.

People have taken this approach before of turning a function a -> b into a -> Prod b Nat, using a state monad, etc. to carry some additional value around for that purpose (like tracking the number of recursive calls). For something more rigorous I think the recommended approach has been to express the problem in terms of a turing machine or some suitable flavor of lambda calculus.
thanks Chris, that makes things a lot clearer. i learned something new here. appreciate both your help and Felix's — this community is great for beginners like me.

If it helps, and slightly orthogonal to the other replies, there is also nothing (uniquely) special about Nat , it is an inductive with a specific set of two constructors (ignoring the optimisations associated with it since its so widely used).

The question of counting succs can be roughly also viewed as delineating or examining in some sense its canonical normal form for an inductive. In general Lean does not have canonicity though, and inductives can be a lot more complicated than the two constructors Nat classically has.

This actually separates the computational aspect (it doesn't have a strict meaning in terms of this form, since you can do this form to any form if you have canonicity but the way it was constructed algorithmically can be arbitrarily long per se, and its never really run anyway most of the time).
